paras: The masked raid on Berry Lawrence's house was a night attack by four masked men on the home of a Black man near Cuthbert, Randolph County, Georgia, on Tuesday, 28 February 1882. Lawrence shot the first raider through the broken door, and the dead man was unmasked as Leonidas Bailey, a young white man of the county. A coroner's jury called the killing justifiable homicide, and the wire story of a Black householder killing a masked white raider ran in papers from Washington to Texas.

According to the wire dispatch from Cuthbert, four masked men came to the house of "a negro living in this county" on Tuesday night and demanded admittance. When they were refused, they broke down the door, and as the first man entered, the householder shot him and the others fled. The Marietta Journal named the householder as Berry Lawrence, "colored," and said he "discharged his gun" at the man coming in.

In the wire version, the Black man and some white neighbors tracked the wounded man for some distance and found his body. The Marietta Journal gave a fuller sequence: Lawrence went to his nearest white neighbor, D. C. Andrews, who found a hat "torn with shot and clotted with blood" and followed a blood trail by torchlight to a body behind the church. Other neighbors arrived at daylight and removed the mask, revealing Leonidas Bailey, while tracks in front of the house showed that four horses and a buggy had been there.

A coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide. The other three men were described as unknown, and the dispatch said the object of their visit had not been learned. No report of arrests or of any further inquiry into the three surviving raiders appears in the coverage.

The story went out as a short Cuthbert dispatch dated March 2 or 3, and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the Washington Evening Star and the Rock Island Argus ran it on March 3. Richmond, Memphis, Savannah, Waco and St. Paul papers followed on March 4, and the St. Landry Democrat in Louisiana carried it a week later. The text varied little, but its headlines differed sharply: the Evening Star called it "A Colored Man's Defence of His Home," the St. Landry Democrat "A Negro Defends His Home and Kills One of His Assailants," and the Waco Daily Examiner "Georgia Ku-Klux."

Other heads treated the householder dismissively, as in the Memphis Daily Appeal's "A Game Darkey" and "A Negro Frightens Masked Men" in The Daily Gazette. Georgia papers focused on the dead man: the Savannah Morning News headed its copy "A Young Planter Shot," and the Marietta Journal, while reporting the justifiable-homicide verdict, described Bailey as about 30 and "sober, industrious and respected in the community."

The Daily Globe's one-line brief placed the raid on Wednesday night, against Tuesday in the full dispatch and the Marietta Journal. The dead man's surname appeared as Bailey, Baily, Bally and Brailay in different papers.

reader.title: Masked raid on Berry Lawrence's house
bases: A band of four masked white or unidentified men rode at night to a Black man's house near Cuthbert and broke down his door after he refused them entry; the householder shot and killed the first man in, and the band's object was never learned (A1, A3, A12).

The only person killed was one of the masked raiders, Leonidas Bailey, shot by the single Black householder as he forced his way in, and a coroner's jury called it justifiable homicide (A1, A12); the band itself killed no one and no report says it threatened to.

The Cuthbert wire (A1, A3, A6, A7) and the Marietta Journal's separate, more detailed account (A12) agree on the masked band, the broken door, the shooting of the first man in and the identity of the dead man.

accounts.label: Cuthbert wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Four masked men broke down a negro's door; he shot the first man in, the rest fled, and the negro with white neighbors tracked the wounded man and found him dead, unmasked as Leonidas Bailey; the object of the visit was unknown.

accounts.label: Marietta Journal
accounts.gist: Names Berry Lawrence as the householder; he went to neighbor D. C. Andrews, who found a bloody hat and the body behind the church; tracks showed four horses and a buggy, and a coroner's jury found justifiable homicide.

framing.detail: Northern and Southern dailies ran the Cuthbert dispatch nearly verbatim under heads such as 'A Georgia Tragedy', 'Shot and Killed' and 'A Masker Shot'.

Some heads cast the shooting as defense of a home ('A Colored Man's Defence of His Home', 'A Negro Defends His Home and Kills One of His Assailants'), one as Klan violence ('Georgia Ku-Klux'), and others in dismissive or racist terms ('A Game Darkey', 'A Negro Frightens Masked Men').
Georgia papers named the dead raider sympathetically: Savannah called him 'A Young Planter', and the Marietta Journal recorded the justifiable-homicide verdict while praising his character.

conflicts.note: The Daily Globe's one-line brief alone says Wednesday; the full wire and the Marietta Journal say Tuesday, the better evidence.

record_check.dossier: One man died, Leonidas Bailey, a white raider; 'Ouidas' is a garble of Savannah's OCR 'Leonidas das Bally'. The targeted Black man was Berry Lawrence, unharmed.
Whitecapping-style night raid by a masked band on a Black man's house; the band killed no one, and one raider was shot by the householder.
none; no killing, attempt or threat to kill by the band is reported

Forced entry (door broken down) by the band; the only killing was of a raider by the householder; no siege; 'pursuit' was the tracking of the wounded raider afterward
